To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
people can perceive and respond to three nonredu ndant signals in vision, audition, and touch at approximately the same time.
people are more likely to fail to detect a cue when three nonredunderant (and unrelated cues are presented to different modalities, and that older adults are particularly susceptible to this effect.

(1) people are more likely to notice and respond to two concurrent cues than three; (2) the presence of three concurrent cues is more disruptive to ongoing task performance than two; (3) older adults are more susceptible to missing cues than younger adults; and (4) the combination of visual and auditory cues are the most disruptive to ongoing task and are the most likely to be missed by older adults.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design and evaluation of multimodal displays that are intended to support multitasking and attention switching.
the design and evaluation of multimodal displays for older adults.
the detection of multiple cues in vision, hearing and touch, and the effects of age-related differences on this ability.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ability to process information from multiple modalities is reduced by aging, and that the ability to do so is further impaired by concurrent task demands.
the results of the present study show that older adults can perceive and process up to two nonredundantly presented visual, auditory, or tactile signals at the same time, but not three.

the results of the present study suggest that older adults have a reduced capacity for processing multiple nonredundantly presented cues in vision, hearing and touch, which is further exacerbated by concurrent task demands.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the ability to perceive and respond to multiple cues presented to different sensory modalities is affected by the number of signals presented at a time, the type of signals presented (e.g., visual, auditory, tactile), and the task demands of the user.

older adults are more likely to be overwhelmed by a large number of cues presented to different modalities, and they may be less likely to detect and respond to the tactile cue when it is presented along with two visual and/or auditory cues.
older adults are more likely to make errors when presented with three nonredunderant signals, but they can still detect all three signals if they are presented one by one.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the number of cues that can be presented concurrently is limited, and this limit is reached sooner for older adults than for younger adults.
designers should be cautious when using multimodal displays and should not assume that the addition of another sensory channel will improve performance.
designers need to be mindful of the number of cues that are being presented to different sensory systems at the same time.
